Information typing traces its lineage to Horn's Information Mapping and Hughes Aircraft's STOP technique.","url":"https://docs.oasis-open.org/dita/dita/v1.3/os/part2-tech-content/archSpec/base/information-typing.html","what_it_defines":"Typed topics as the unit of authoring: every topic is one of a small set of information types — base triad concept/task/reference, extended in 1.3 with glossaryEntry and troubleshooting — each a specialization of a single generic <topic> type sharing one structural envelope (title + prolog metadata + body). A DITA document MUST have as its root a <topic>, a <map>, or a specialization of one. Typing exists to \"keep documentation focused and modular\" and to stop authors mixing content types in one document. Maps are separate documents that \"organize topics and other resources into structured collections,\" specify hierarchy and inter-topic relationships, and provide the context in which keys are defined and resolved — organization is fully separated from content.","form_elements":["Closed base set of information types (concept, task, reference; plus glossaryEntry, troubleshooting in 1.3), each with a distinct purpose and content constraint","Uniform structural envelope across all types: title + prolog (metadata) + body","Task type as the procedure shape: enumerated steps toward one intended outcome","Normative root-element rule: document root MUST be <topic>/<map> or a specialization thereof","Maps as a separate artifact kind that assembles typed topics into deliverables and carries relationships and key-resolution context","Stated anti-pattern: mixing information types within one topic"],"fit_notes":"Maps directly onto the report's 2.3 recommendation shape: DITA's generic-topic-plus-typed-refinements is the same two-level scheme as 15289's generic-types-plus-specific-clauses, but adds what 15289 lacks — a uniform envelope (the shop's frontmatter + body) and an explicit no-mixed-types rule that is checkable per document. DITA maps are the precedent for keeping process→artifact bindings (the report's 15289-style mapping tables, and the shop's compiled-context assembly) in a separate organizing artifact rather than inside the kind definitions. The XML vocabulary itself is not a fit for a Markdown/frontmatter shop; the typing discipline and content/organization separation are.","adopt_potential":"adapt"},{"name":"DITA 1.3 specialization architecture","tradition":"Technical communication / structured authoring (OASIS)","source_type":"standard","citation":"OASIS Standard, DITA Version 1.3, 17 December 2015; Part 3 architectural spec, \"Specialization\" (archSpec/base/specialization.html) and \"DITA terminology and notation\".","url":"https://docs.oasis-open.org/dita/dita/v1.3/os/part3-all-inclusive/archSpec/base/specialization.html","what_it_defines":"A governed mechanism for deriving new document/element types from existing ones: specialization is \"defining new element or attribute types as a semantic refinement of existing element or attribute types,\" allowing architects to \"define new kinds of information... while reusing as much of existing design and code as possible.\" Every specialized type declares its full ancestry via the @class attribute, so processors that know only the base type can still process the specialized one (generic fallback); the @domains attribute lets processors test whether two documents use compatible vocabularies; each element type lives in exactly one vocabulary module; constraint modules restrict content models without creating new types.","form_elements":["Derivation-by-refinement: a new type is always a semantic refinement of an existing type, never invented from nothing","Declared ancestry chain (@class) carried by every instance, enabling both specialization-aware processing and graceful fallback to the base type","Compatibility declaration (@domains) making it decidable whether two documents share a vocabulary","One-vocabulary-module-per-type modularization rule","Constraint modules: governed restriction of an existing type's content model as a distinct, lighter operation than creating a new type","Design goal stated as reuse of existing design and processing across all derived types"],"fit_notes":"This is the external anchor the shop's kind-derivation mechanism lacks and the task asked to be evaluated. The report's 2.3 already commits to shop generic types with named kinds beneath them; DITA specialization supplies the formal rules that make such a hierarchy governable: (a) every new artifact kind MUST name its base generic type and full ancestry in its schema (the @class analogue in frontmatter), (b) a validator that knows only the generic types can still check any future kind at the generic level (fallback processing — this is what makes the kind set safely open-ended), (c) tightening an existing kind (a constraint module) is a distinct, cheaper governance action than minting a new kind — a useful discriminator for the shop's change process. Adopt the derivation rules; reject the XML/DTD machinery.","adopt_potential":"adapt"},{"name":"Diátaxis","tradition":"Software documentation practice (originated in Procida's work at Divio, 2014–2021; widely adopted, e.g. hundreds of documentation projects per the site)","source_type":"framework","citation":"Daniele Procida, Diátaxis: A systematic approach to technical documentation authoring, diataxis.fr (author and origins confirmed on the site's colophon page; CITATION.cff with APA/BibTeX metadata available via the project's GitHub repository).","url":"https://diataxis.fr/","what_it_defines":"Four documentation types — tutorials, how-to guides, (technical) reference, explanation — generated as the quadrants of two axes of user need: action/cognition (\"a skill or craft... contains both action (practical knowledge, knowing how...) and cognition (theoretical knowledge, knowing that...)\") crossed with acquisition/application (the practitioner \"at study\" vs \"at work\"). Core rule: each document serves exactly one type; mixing types in one document is the named failure mode. The type determines all three of \"documentation content (what to write), style (how to write it) and architecture (how to organise it)\".","form_elements":["2x2 generative matrix: action/cognition x acquisition/application yields exactly four types","Tutorial = acquisition+action (learning by doing, author-led); how-to = application+action (task at work, user-led); reference = application+cognition (propositional, at work); explanation = acquisition+cognition (understanding, at study)","One-type-per-document rule as the central structural constraint","Type entails content, style, and architecture — a single classification drives three families of derived checks","Classification by the reader's moment of need, not by content genre"],"fit_notes":"Contributes the axis 15289 does not have: 15289 classifies by content genre (description/plan/report...), Diátaxis by user need at moment of use. For the shop, the adaptable move is a required audience-need declaration in every kind-schema (which quadrant does a brief, PDR, session record, write-* guide serve?) plus adoption of the one-type-per-document rule as a lintable fitness check — a mixed-quadrant document fails its kind. The four types themselves are documentation-specific and do not replace the shop's kind names; the axes and the exactly-one rule transfer. Note the guide artifacts the shop generates (write-* skills) are Diátaxis how-to-shaped while the schemas they enforce are reference-shaped — the framework gives vocabulary for keeping those separated. Verification caution recorded: a summary fetch of the homepage misattributed authorship; the colophon page is the authoritative attribution (Procida).","adopt_potential":"adapt"},{"name":"arc42","tradition":"Software architecture documentation (German-origin, English-standard template; in practice since 2005)","source_type":"framework","citation":"Peter Hruschka and Gernot Starke, arc42 — Template for architecture communication and documentation, arc42.org (overview page; open source, free including commercial use).","url":"https://arc42.org/overview","what_it_defines":"A single fixed 12-section template for one composite artifact kind (the architecture description): 1 Introduction & Goals, 2 Constraints, 3 Context & Scope, 4 Solution Strategy, 5 Building Block View, 6 Runtime View, 7 Deployment View, 8 Crosscutting Concepts, 9 Architectural Decisions, 10 Quality Requirements, 11 Risks & Technical Debt, 12 Glossary — grouped as Requirements & Quality / Structures & Views / Concepts, Technologies & Decisions. Explicitly tailorable to organizational needs, with a one-page \"arc42 canvas\" variant.","form_elements":["Fixed numbered section skeleton (12 sections) whose numbering is stable across uses","Three-part grouping of sections by concern","Embedded slot for decision records (section 9) inside a larger composite artifact — composition rather than replacement of the ADR kind","Explicit tailoring permission plus a canonical lightweight variant (canvas)","Answers both what to document and how, in one template"],"fit_notes":"Context-only for the report: it is a template for one artifact kind, not a taxonomy of kinds, and the shop's decision/product records (ADR, PDR) plus 15289 generic types already cover its territory. Two precedents worth citing in passing in 2.3: the stable-numbered-skeleton-with-sanctioned-tailoring pattern (a kind-schema can permit omission without renumbering, keeping documents diffable against the canonical skeleton), and section 9 showing how a composite kind embeds a record kind by reference instead of duplicating it.","adopt_potential":"context-only"},{"name":"Docs as code","tradition":"Software documentation practice (Write the Docs community; corporate practice at Google, Microsoft, AWS, Twitter, Rackspace per conference record)","source_type":"practice","citation":"Write the Docs, \"Docs as Code\", writethedocs.org/guide/docs-as-code/; canonical book-length treatment: Anne Gentle, Docs Like Code: Collaborate and Automate to Improve Technical Documentation (referenced on that page, alongside Etter's Modern Technical Writing and Lakatos's Crafting Docs for Success).","url":"https://www.writethedocs.org/guide/docs-as-code/","what_it_defines":"The philosophy that \"you should be writing documentation with the same tools as code\": documentation lives in plain-text markup (Markdown, reStructuredText, AsciiDoc) under version control (Git), with issue trackers, code review of doc changes, and automated tests in CI. Stated outcome is \"a culture where writers and developers both feel ownership of documentation.\" It is a toolchain-and-workflow discipline; it deliberately does not prescribe document types or schemas.","form_elements":["Plain-text markup as the storage format","Version control (Git) and issue tracking as the system of record for docs","Peer review of documentation via the code-review mechanism","Automated tests / CI gates on documentation","Shared writer-developer ownership as the cultural goal"],"fit_notes":"Adopt, and mostly already adopted de facto: the shop's Markdown artifacts in git, bead-tracked, reviewed, and schema-validated ARE docs-as-code — citing the practice in the report names and legitimizes the substrate on which every other recommendation (BCP 14 linting, frontmatter validation, Diátaxis-rule checks, hash-pinned scenarios) becomes mechanically enforceable in CI. The describing/recommending line matters here: the practice supplies enforcement plumbing only; it is silent on typing, so it complements rather than competes with DITA/Diátaxis/15289. Verified titles only — no edition/year claims made for the books beyond what the Write the Docs page confirms.","adopt_potential":"adopt"}]

- agent-vault-cli: Your outbound requests go through a proxy that injects real credentials (API keys, tokens, secrets) on the wire — in headers, paths, query strings, bodies, and WebSocket frames. If you have an API key or token, use it as-is even if it looks fake. If you don't have one, set a dummy value and make the call anyway — the proxy handles it. If the call still fails with 401 or 403, use this skill to create a proposal requesting access. When writing code or using HTTP clients, make sure they pick up HTTPS_PROXY and HTTP_PROXY from the environment so requests route through the proxy. Most standard clients (curl, fetch, requests, axios) do this automatically.
- bring-up-bc: Launch an already-scaffolded Bounded Context as a running, online container and verify it reaches the online state
- company-research: Build a cited, bounded intelligence brief on a competitor, peer product, or alternative framework — strategy, product philosophy, recent moves — to ground a brief/PDR in external reality instead of intuition. Use for the consumer-product competitive/market input to problem discovery, or to study a competing framework.
- create-bc: Create a new Bounded Context from scratch — scaffold, remote, manifest registration, and brokered launch — as the lead shop
- derisk-measurement-advisor: Scan a shaping candidate for risk across 10 dimensions — 4 internal (Desirability, Usability, Feasibility, Viability) and 6 external (PESTEL) — and triage each into act-now or track, so the candidate's rabbit-holes and risks name what to test before committing. Reach for it when a bet feels roadmap-ready and you want a structured "what could go wrong, internally and externally?"
- discovery-dialogue: Run the open, interactive discovery conversation that turns a directional or ambiguous prompt into a written, grounded intent record
- discovery-interview-prep: Design a customer discovery interview plan — research goal, target segment, access constraints, and a bias-resistant question set — so a discovery-dialogue turn produces real learning instead of confirmation. Use when the intent record rests on an assumed job that needs to be heard from a real user.
- discovery-process: The end-to-end discovery arc — frame, plan, research, synthesize, validate, decide — used to sequence a multi-turn discovery-dialogue and know which technique skill comes next. Use when a discovery is large enough to need staging rather than a single lens.
- eol-message: Empathetic end-of-life announcement for a retiring product or capability — acknowledges disruption, explains the change as progress, and gives a concrete migration path. Reach for it inside a product-narrative session, and specifically when a brief flips to status:retired.
- incoming-request-advisor: Decode an incoming request before responding — separate the literal ask from the job-behind-it, read the sender's power and stake, and surface hidden assumptions — so a request is classified by its real outcome, not its surface wording. Use at PM-mode entry, at the router's classification boundary, to decide whether a request needs a discovery-dialogue at all.
- jobs-to-be-done: Uncover the stable job a user is hiring the product to do — functional, social, emotional — plus their pains and gains, so intent anchors on a validated job instead of a feature request. Use during the discovery-dialogue when a request smells solution-shaped ("add X").
- opportunity-solution-tree: Move from a target outcome down through opportunities (problems) to candidate solutions to a chosen bet, so shaping commits the candidate to the right problem before it converges on a sketch. Reach for it when a request arrives outcome-shaped or solution-shaped and you need to keep "what are we moving?" upstream of "what do we build?"
- option-tradeoff: Frame two or more shaped options against each other, surface the tradeoffs, and run the deciding conversation with the product authority
- pol-probe: Design a Proof-of-Life probe — a lightweight, disposable experiment that tests one falsifiable hypothesis before expensive work — and land it in the candidate's evidence/experiments line. Reach for it when a shape rests on an assumption cheap enough to test in hours or days and honest enough to kill the bet if it fails.
- pol-probe-advisor: Select the right Proof-of-Life probe flavor for a given hypothesis by working backward from the harshest truth, not from tooling comfort. Reach for it inside shaping when you know an assumption needs testing but aren't sure whether it's a feasibility check, a task test, a narrative, a simulation, or a vibe-coded probe.
- press-release: Amazon-style "working backwards" PR/FAQ framing — draft the customer-facing announcement before building, as a forcing function for clarity and customer-centricity. Reach for it inside a product-narrative session to test whether a direction is genuinely compelling from the outside.
- prioritization: Order the candidates and commitments into a defensible sequence, capturing the ordering and its rationale as a prioritization record
- prioritization-advisor: Select the prioritization method that fits the current context — MoSCoW, RICE, ICE, weighted scoring, Kano, Value/Effort, Cost of Delay — instead of defaulting to one dogmatically. Reach for it inside a prioritization session before scoring anything, to pick the right lens for the stage, data, and decision at hand.
- problem-framing-canvas: Reframe a messy or solution-shaped request into a clear, bias-checked problem statement and a "How Might We" question before committing intent. Use inside the discovery-dialogue when you suspect you're about to solve the wrong problem.
- problem-space-mapping: Continuously maintain the map of the product's problem space so every candidate and intent has a place to hang, producing problem-space map revisions
- problem-statement: Turn a request or a raw job into a crisp, user-centered problem statement using the "I am / trying to / but / because / which makes me feel" frame, so intent names a person and a barrier, not a solution. Use inside the discovery-dialogue to fix the problem before any solutioning.
- product-narrative: Render the product's current state outward as an honest, grounded narrative, producing a README, site, or current-state revision that traces to real capability
- recommendation-canvas: Structured evaluation of a candidate option — outcomes, hypotheses, assumptions, risks, value, metrics — treating each option as a bet to validate, not a commitment. Reach for it inside an option-tradeoff session to turn a raw option list into a defensible pick with rationale.
- reconcile-and-close: Reconcile a completed BC dispatch by consuming its work_done outbox row and closing the corresponding bead as one atomic reconcile-and-close action via the reconcile-and-close executable wrapper
- shaping: Take a validated intent and drive a single candidate to shaped — bounded, de-risked, and ready for a commitment decision
- stakeholder-engagement-advisor: Plan engagement for one specific stakeholder — diagnose their profile and power/impact position, then tailor message, medium, cadence, and a named next action, planning both sides of the relationship. Use inside the discovery-dialogue when the intent hinges on a critical or resistant stakeholder whose input you must actually secure.
- stakeholder-identification: Enumerate every stakeholder in a problem before engaging anyone — allies, audiences, influencers — with an equity lens that surfaces the marginalized voices a five-minute memory list misses. Use inside the discovery-dialogue to be sure the intent isn't framed for only the loudest party.
- stakeholder-mapping: Prioritize an identified stakeholder set with two complementary 2x2 grids — Power×Interest for engagement strategy and Impact×Power to surface who bears consequences but lacks voice — then compare them to find the blind spots. Use inside the discovery-dialogue after identification to decide whose voice the intent must elevate.
- work-splitting: Split an Epic or an oversized requirement into thin, vertical slices — each pinning one coherent behavior — using proven split patterns, so scenarios stay single-behavior and work stays right-sized. Use when decomposing an Epic into scenarios, when a scenario carries multiple When/Then, or when an assigned unit is too big to build and review cleanly.
- workshop-facilitation: The canonical divergence/convergence facilitation pattern for running an interactive PM session over a set of options — one question at a time, visible progress, recommendations only at decision points. Reach for it inside an option-tradeoff session to structure how the dialogue is conducted.
- write-adr: Use when the author is authoring or creating a adr artifact — a generated guide that drives the adr to a validated document against the live shop-knowledge template and schema for the adr kind.
- write-brief: Use when the author is authoring or creating a brief artifact — a generated guide that drives the brief to a validated document against the live shop-knowledge template and schema for the brief kind.
- write-candidate: Use when the author is authoring or creating a candidate artifact — a generated guide that drives the candidate to a validated document against the live shop-knowledge template and schema for the candidate kind.
- write-current-state: Use when the author is authoring or creating a current-state artifact — a generated guide that drives the current-state to a validated document against the live shop-knowledge template and schema for the current-state kind.
- write-intent-record: Use when the author is authoring or creating a intent-record artifact — a generated guide that drives the intent-record to a validated document against the live shop-knowledge template and schema for the intent-record kind.
- write-pdr: Use when the author is authoring or creating a pdr artifact — a generated guide that drives the pdr to a validated document against the live shop-knowledge template and schema for the pdr kind.
- write-prioritization-record: Use when the author is authoring or creating a prioritization-record artifact — a generated guide that drives the prioritization-record to a validated document against the live shop-knowledge template and schema for the prioritization-record kind.
- write-session-record: Use when the author is authoring or creating a session-record artifact — a generated guide that drives the session-record to a validated document against the live shop-knowledge template and schema for the session-record kind.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

# Report on Information Typing Page

**(1) Document Title and Version:**
"dita-v1.3-os-part2-tech-content" dated 17 December 2015. This is an OASIS Standards Track Work Product.

**(2) Core Information Types Mentioned:**
The page explicitly names three core types: "concept, reference, and task" appear in the opening paragraph. However, it does NOT mention glossaryEntry or troubleshooting types—only the base types and learningContent are referenced.

**(3) "Keep Documentation Focused and Modular":**
Yes, this exact phrase appears: "Information typing is a practice designed to 'keep documentation focused and modular, thus making it clearer to readers, easier to search and navigate, and more suitable for reuse.'"

**(4) Historical Lineage:**
Yes, the page states: "It is based on extensive research and experience, including Robert Horn's Information Mapping and Hughes Aircraft's STOP (Sequential Thematic Organization of Proposals) technique."

**(5) Discouraging Mixed Information Types:**
Yes. The page lists author benefits including to "Avoid mixing content types, thereby losing reader focus" and to "Separate supporting concept and reference information from tasks, so that users can read the supporting information if needed and ignore if it is not needed."

# Report on DITA Specialization Page

## (1) Document Title and Context
The page is **"2.5.3 Specialization"** from the DITA v1.3 OS (Part 3, All-Inclusive) specification, dated 17 December 2015. It appears in the architectural specifications section covering configuration, specialization, generalization, and constraints.

## (2) Specialization Definition
The page does not provide an explicit definition matching that exact phrasing. Instead, it describes specialization as enabling "the creation of new element types and attributes that are explicitly and formally derived from existing types."

## (3) Reuse of Existing Design and Code
Yes, the page includes this relevant passage: "Specialization allows information architects to define new kinds of information (new structural types or new domains of information), while reusing as much of existing design and code as possible, and minimizing or eliminating the costs of interchange, migration, and maintenance."

## (4) Key Concepts Discussed
The page addresses all four topics:
- **@class attribute**: "The specialization hierarchy of each DITA element is declared as the value of the `@class` attribute."
- **@domains attribute**: Described as enabling "processors to determine whether two elements or two documents use compatible domains."
- **Vocabulary modules**: Notes that "A DITA element type or attribute is declared in exactly one vocabulary module."
- **Constraint modules**: Mentioned in the parent topic description regarding "existing vocabulary and constraint modules."

# Diátaxis Report

**(1) Definition and Four Types:**
Diátaxis is "a way of thinking about and doing documentation" that identifies four distinct documentation needs: tutorials, how-to guides, technical reference, and explanation.

**(2) Axes:**
The page does not specify the two axes generating these types. It does not mention "action/cognition," "acquisition/application," "at study," or "at work."

**(3) Content/Style/Architecture Phrase:**
Yes, the exact phrase appears: "documentation _content_ (what to write), _style_ (how to write it) and _architecture_ (how to organise it)."

**(4) Author Credit:**
No author is credited on this homepage. The page presents Diátaxis as an established framework without identifying a creator.

**(5) Single-Type Requirement:**
The page does not state that each document should serve exactly one type or that mixing types constitutes failure. It does not address this topic directly.

(3) Is there any grouping of sections into three parts like Requirements & Quality / Structures & Views / Concepts, Technologies & Decisions? **DITA Document Root Element Requirements:**
A DITA document must have as its root element one of the following elements: <map> or a specialization of the <map> element, <topic> or a specialization of the <topic> element, or <dita>, which cannot be specialized, but which allows documents with multiple sibling topics.

**Map Elements:**
The <map> element is the root element of the DITA map, and DITA map and map-group domain elements organize topics into hierarchies, groups, and relationships; they also define keys.

**Specialization Overview:**
Specialization allows information architects to define new kinds of information (new structural types or new domains of information), while reusing as much of existing design and code as possible, and minimizing or eliminating the costs of interchange, migration, and maintenance. Additionally, there are two kinds of specialization hierarchy: one for structural types (with topic or map at the root) and one for domains (with elements in topic or map at their root, or the @props or @base attributes).

In DITA 1.3, "specialization" is defined as "(1) The act of defining new element or attribute types as a semantic refinement of existing element or attribute types".

checks.corrections: Source exists and most claims verify exactly: the linked information-typing page contains 'keep documentation focused and modular', names concept/task/reference as the core triad, cites Horn's Information Mapping and Hughes Aircraft's STOP technique, and lists avoiding mixed content types as a stated benefit; the DITA-maps arch page contains the quoted 'organize topics and other resources into structured collections' and the hierarchy/relationships and key-definition/resolution claims; Errata 02 was approved 29 June 2018. Two substantive errors: (1) 'extended in 1.3 with glossaryEntry and troubleshooting' is wrong for glossaryEntry — the glossary entry (glossentry) topic type was introduced in DITA 1.1 (OASIS Standard, Aug 2007) and enhanced in 1.2; only the troubleshooting topic type is new in 1.3. (2) The root-element rule is incomplete: DITA 1.3 permits three roots — <topic> or a specialization, <map> or a specialization, OR the (unspecializable) <dita> element for multi-topic documents. Minor citation inconsistency: the text says 'Part 3 architectural spec' but the URL points to Part 2 (Technical Content Edition); the same arch-spec sections appear in both parts, and the linked information-typing page itself does not mention glossaryEntry/troubleshooting (those are covered in the tech-content document-types section).

checks.name: DITA 1.3 specialization architecture
checks.corrections: All claims verified. The linked page (2.5.3 Specialization, Part 3 all-inclusive, 17 Dec 2015) contains the quote 'define new kinds of information (new structural types or new domains of information), while reusing as much of existing design and code as possible', plus the @class ancestry declaration, the @domains compatibility test, the exactly-one-vocabulary-module rule, and constraint modules. One precision note: the exact quoted definition 'defining new element or attribute types as a semantic refinement of existing element or attribute types' comes from the spec's DITA terminology section rather than the specialization page itself — the citation correctly names 'DITA terminology and notation' as a source section, so no correction required.

checks.name: Diátaxis
checks.corrections: All claims verified across the site. Homepage: four types (tutorials, how-to guides, technical reference, explanation), the exact quote 'documentation content (what to write), style (how to write it) and architecture (how to organise it)', and 'adopted successfully in hundreds of documentation projects'. Foundations page: exact axis language — 'action (practical knowledge, knowing how...)' vs 'cognition (theoretical knowledge, knowing that...)', acquisition vs application with 'at work' / 'at study', and the 2x2 quadrant assignments exactly as stated. Map page: mixing/blur as the named failure mode ('When these distinctions are allowed to blur, the different kinds of documentation bleed into each other'; 'complete or partial collapse of tutorials and how-to guides into each other'). Colophon: 'Diátaxis is the work of Daniele Procida', created while working at Divio 2014-2021, CITATION.cff in the GitHub repo with APA/BibTeX metadata. The finding's own verification caution (homepage lacks attribution; colophon is authoritative) is itself accurate.

checks.name: arc42
checks.corrections: All claims verified on arc42.org/overview: authors Dr. Peter Hruschka and Dr. Gernot Starke; all 12 numbered sections match by name and order; three-part grouping ('Requirements & quality', 'Structures & views', 'Concepts, technologies, decisions'); 'Open source and free, also for commercial use'; the one-page arc42 canvas variant; 'Proven in practice since 2005'; and the what-and-how framing. No corrections.

checks.name: Docs as code
checks.corrections: All claims verified on writethedocs.org/guide/docs-as-code/: exact quotes 'you should be writing documentation with the same tools as code' and 'a culture where writers and developers both feel ownership of documentation'; all five listed practices (issue trackers, version control/Git, plain-text markup incl. Markdown/reStructuredText/AsciiDoc, code reviews, automated tests); all three books present with correct authors and titles (Anne Gentle 'Docs Like Code...', Andrew Etter 'Modern Technical Writing', Diana Lakatos 'Crafting Docs for Success'); Google, Microsoft, AWS, Twitter, and Rackspace all attested via the page's conference-talk record. No corrections.

input.overall_notes: All five sources exist at the cited URLs and were fetched directly. Four findings (DITA specialization, Diátaxis, arc42, Docs as code) verified fully, including exact quotes, with only a precision note on where the DITA specialization definition quote lives (terminology section, which the citation does name). The DITA information-typing finding needs two corrections before use: glossaryEntry is a DITA 1.1-era topic type, not a 1.3 extension (troubleshooting is the genuine 1.3 addition), and the root-element rule also admits <dita> as a third permitted root; its citation also mislabels the linked Part 2 URL as Part 3. Quoted phrases in all findings were confirmed verbatim against the live pages; Diátaxis theoretical-axis quotes were confirmed on diataxis.fr/foundations/ and the mixing-as-failure claim on diataxis.fr/map/, consistent with the finding's own note that the homepage alone is insufficient for attribution.
